independence: International registry, regulation, science, encyclopaedias and local testimony converge.
missing_definition: The Riesling word here is historical nomenclature and does not establish kinship with Rhine Riesling.
editor_conclusion: Keep the historical synonym claim and explicitly separate it from Rhine Riesling.

comparison: The official 1983 EEC regulation directly prints BANATSKI RIZLING and KREACA together in the Yugoslav table.
independence: Primary legal document; modern registry and scientific synonym evidence independently agree.
missing_definition: Describe the document as an administrative list for wine-name presentation, not as genetic proof.
editor_conclusion: Keep with the regulation number and its limited evidentiary meaning.

comparison: The current official product page lists seven grapes, and independent Serbian specialist reports describe the same multi-variety blend.
independence: Official current page plus multiple independent media sources converge.
missing_definition: The label is a wine name; Kreaca is only one component and current public percentages are not supplied.
editor_conclusion: Keep «многосортовой купаж» and add the exact seven varieties.

comparison: Official and independent pages clearly use Banatski Rizling as a durable commercial label/brand. No selected primary trademark-register record proves a current registered word mark owned by Drašković.
independence: Commercial use is multiply documented; the narrower legal proposition lacks primary registry evidence.
missing_definition: Russian «торговая марка» can mean brand colloquially or registered trademark legally; the book does not distinguish them.
editor_conclusion: Change to «коммерческое название/бренд вина» unless a current Serbian trademark-register record is cited.

comparison: The historical synonym and the present seven-variety wine are independently and directly documented, so the two-meaning warning is substantively correct.
independence: Registry/regulatory/scientific sources establish the cultivar meaning; the official producer and wine press establish the product meaning.
missing_definition: The second object includes Kreaca but is not identical to it, so this is polysemy/homonymy in market use rather than two unrelated strings.
editor_conclusion: Keep the distinction prominently; it is the strongest and most useful statement in the card.

comparison: The 1964 manual gives 18–20% sugar, while the Gudurica study supplies observed clone and annual ranges around that baseline.
independence: Historical technical literature and modern measured peer-reviewed research converge but show variation.
missing_definition: Specify that these are must sugar percentages under the cited studies, not current legal minimums or universal Brix values.
editor_conclusion: Add the 18–20% baseline only with the 17.6–22.6% clone range or an explicit variability warning.

comparison: The historical manual consistently gives 10–12% alcohol and 5–6‰ acidity for Kreaca wine; no current monovarietal product specification was found to update it.
independence: Direct technical source, compatible with the book's restrained style but not independently replicated in a modern bottle.
missing_definition: Historical per-mille acidity is conventionally read approximately as g/L total acidity in this context; retain source attribution and date.
editor_conclusion: Use as a dated traditional technical profile, not a modern product guarantee.

comparison: The old manual says characteristic varietal aroma, while RTV says no strong aroma and CEVVIN calls the berry neutral. These positions agree on restrained intensity more than on complete aromatic absence.
independence: Historical technical and modern regional evidence describe different stages and can coexist.
missing_definition: Neutral grape flesh, low aromatic intensity and a subtle characteristic wine aroma are distinct concepts.
missing_descriptors: The safest synthesis is «сдержанный, но сортовой аромат», not an invented fruit list for monovarietal Kreaca.
editor_conclusion: Add the distinction to prevent readers from treating neutral berry as aroma-free wine.

comparison: The official current page and several independent product reports agree on Italian Riesling, Rhine Riesling, Župljanka, Kreaca, Smederevka, Rkatsiteli and Chasselas.
independence: Direct producer-group record plus independent specialist/retail repetition.
missing_definition: Public current percentages are absent; older statements that Grašac was at least 50% are historical and should not be silently carried into the present recipe.
editor_conclusion: Add the seven varieties without percentages.

comparison: The current official page directly gives dry white style and 11.5% alcohol; the current retail card matches it.
independence: Primary product page with current secondary confirmation.
editor_conclusion: Add as dated current product facts if the wine receives a fuller subentry.

comparison: Vino & Fino reports citrus and yellow fruit, Vino.rs tropical fruit, and the current retail note white peach, tropical fruit and citrus. The common core is fresh fruit/citrus rather than every listed aroma.
independence: Two independent specialist tastings and one commercial note broadly converge.
missing_definition: Descriptor lists are vintage- and bottle-specific and should be attributed to the modern blend, never to Kreaca alone.
missing_descriptors: Consensus set: yellow/white stone fruit, tropical fruit and citrus; exact emphasis varies.
editor_conclusion: Add only as an attributed modern Banatski Rizling profile with a vintage/date caveat.

comparison: Freshness, harmony and balanced/lively acidity recur across Vino.rs, Vino & Fino and the current retail note.
independence: Independent specialist sources and a current product card converge on structure.
missing_definition: Freshness is sensory and can arise from acidity, aroma and serving context; it is not an analytical acid value by itself.
missing_descriptors: Fresh, harmonious, balanced acidity.
editor_conclusion: Use this as the strongest consensus description of the current blend.

comparison: Solid body and slight butteriness appear in the single detailed Vino.rs tasting; other sources mention structure but do not independently repeat butteriness.
independence: One direct specialist tasting, with only partial structural corroboration.
missing_definition: Butteriness can derive from fermentation/lees/oak processes, but no source here proves the cause.
missing_descriptors: Moderately substantial body; possible slight buttery texture/aroma for the tasted release.
editor_conclusion: Include only as a dated Vino.rs bottle note, not consensus or cultivar character.

comparison: Vino.rs says the tropical aromas do not linger long, while Vino & Fino calls the length decent. Both point to a moderate rather than long finish.
independence: Two independent Serbian specialist tastings broadly agree.
missing_definition: Finish length remains a sensory judgement and may vary by vintage and serving conditions.
missing_descriptors: Moderate/decent finish length.
editor_conclusion: Optional attributed descriptor for the current blend; do not generalize to Kreaca.

comparison: CEVVIN and SerbianWine.rs describe broad Balkan distribution; English Wikipedia and international references confirm the Smederevka/Dimyat identity but emphasize Bulgaria and North Macedonia differently.
independence: National centre, requested Wikipedia and international wine references agree on wide distribution despite origin framing conflicts.
missing_definition: «Повсюду» should mean broadly Balkan, not literally universal or evenly planted within Serbia.
editor_conclusion: Replace with «широко распространена на Балканах» and name the main countries.

comparison: English Wikipedia calls Dimyat wines very aromatic, while German Wikipedia gives no comparable sensory claim; Falstaff calls them rather neutral, technical Serbian material calls the must neutral, and modern Serbian sources list distinct aromas.
independence: The conflict spans encyclopaedic, technical and tasting corpora and partly reflects grape/must versus finished-wine and basic versus ambitious styles.
missing_definition: Neutral must, low-intensity young wine and aroma-bearing finished wine are different propositions.
missing_descriptors: Lemon/citrus, herbs, white flowers and conditional vanilla; some bottles show orchard fruit or lees-derived notes.
editor_conclusion: Do not print bare «нейтральная»; use «сусло нейтральное, базовые вина сдержанные, но современные вина могут быть явно ароматными».

comparison: CEVVIN, English Wikipedia, Falstaff and Serbian technical material consistently describe high yield potential and risk of overcropping.
independence: National, encyclopaedic and specialist sources converge.
missing_definition: High genetic yield potential becomes actual overcropping only under pruning, site and crop-management conditions.
editor_conclusion: Keep «очень урожайная» and add the yield-control consequence.

comparison: CEVVIN gives must acidity up to about 9 g/L; the technical profile gives 7–9 g/L must and 6–8 g/L wine; peer-reviewed six-vintage wines span 4.8–7.2 g/L and modern tastings repeatedly describe fresh acidity.
independence: National technical, peer-reviewed analytical and sensory sources converge.
missing_definition: Total acidity is an analytical value and should not automatically be translated as sourness.
missing_descriptors: Fresh, brisk or crisp acidity is the recurring sensory correlate.
editor_conclusion: Keep noticeable acidity, but cite a range rather than one unidentified result.

comparison: Technical sources give 9–11% for basic wine, Rubin 10.5%, and the six-vintage study 10.21–11.0%; Biser and premium still wines show that higher alcohol is possible.
independence: Historical/technical, current product and peer-reviewed measurements converge for the basic style.
missing_definition: The statement is style-dependent, not a hard varietal ceiling.
editor_conclusion: Use «часто умеренный алкоголь в базовых версиях» and avoid universal low-alcohol wording.

comparison: Rubin confirms 10.5% without acidity; the peer-reviewed study spans values around both numbers but does not publish the exact pair as the same identified sample in the material selected here.
independence: The current producer and independent study concern different wines and cannot be spliced into one analysis.
missing_definition: A valid analytical citation needs producer, wine, vintage, laboratory/method and whether acidity is expressed as tartaric acid.
editor_conclusion: Delete the exact pair until the original analysis is identified; replace with sourced ranges.

comparison: Multiple Serbian sources strongly associate Smederevka with cold summer špricer, but targeted exact-phrase searches did not establish «king of spritzer» as a recognized cultivar nickname.
independence: Producer, national press and multilingual beverage references converge on the practice, not the title.
missing_definition: A metaphor created by the book should be marked as editorial rather than presented as an inherited nickname.
editor_conclusion: Change «прозвище» to an attributed editorial formula or simply say «классическое вино для шприцера».

comparison: High initial acidity makes a diluted drink plausibly taste fresher, but all acid concentrations fall on dilution and matrix effects on aroma are complex. No direct comparative trial shows a unique Smederevka advantage.
independence: General peer-reviewed chemistry qualifies the mechanism; local tradition provides no controlled test.
missing_definition: «Каркас сохраняется» requires a sensory threshold, dilution ratio and comparison wines.
editor_conclusion: Present as an author tasting inference, not an established technological explanation.

comparison: Technical Serbian material, NIN, Falstaff and two commercial Serbian sparkling examples all confirm suitability. The current public CEVVIN page itself does not mention sparkling wine, so the exact attribution needs the cited publication rather than the webpage.
independence: Technical references, independent tasting and current products converge on practical potential.
missing_definition: Potential is demonstrated by successful products, not by acidity alone; distinguish traditional method from generic sparkling production.
editor_conclusion: Keep the potential claim, cite the exact CEVVIN publication if attributing it to the Centre, and add Biser as evidence.

comparison: Biser is current and Emporio is documented, so the use is real; the small visible set suggests a niche, but no label count, volume or market share proves «almost unused».
independence: Producer and independent media/database evidence establish multiple examples but not national prevalence.
missing_definition: Underuse must be measured against planted area, still-wine volume or number of producers.
editor_conclusion: Replace with «пока нишевое применение» and avoid an unquantified near-zero claim.

comparison: CEVVIN directly links allowed high yield with low sugar accumulation and must acidity around 9 g/L; the secondary technical profile independently gives 16–20% sugar and 7–9 g/L acids.
independence: Current national centre and historical/technical reproduction converge.
missing_definition: Yield level and ripeness year must accompany analytical ranges.
editor_conclusion: Add this crop-load mechanism because it explains the basic style better than an isolated analysis.

comparison: CEVVIN, NIN, SerbianWine.rs, Mišić and technical references repeatedly use light, fresh, drinkable, refreshing or crisp language.
independence: National technical, independent press, directory and producer sources converge.
missing_definition: These describe the common young style, not every premium, orange, barrel or sparkling version.
missing_descriptors: Light, fresh, drinkable, refreshing, crisp.
editor_conclusion: Add as the main consensus sensory definition for basic Smederevka.

comparison: NIN foregrounds lemon; Falstaff's Biser gives lime zest and citrus finish, while other modern examples also use citrus. Not every technical profile lists a named fruit.
independence: Broad national profile and independent bottle tasting converge.
missing_definition: Use as a recurring modern descriptor, not a chemically measured or universal marker.
missing_descriptors: Lemon, lime zest and general citrus.
editor_conclusion: Add citrus with source attribution and style/vintage caveat.

comparison: NIN gives subtle herbs and white flowers; current Biser gives dried flowers. The recurrence supports a floral/herbal family but not one invariant exact flower.
independence: General profile and current producer product overlap partially.
missing_definition: Floral and herbal are descriptor families; retain the source-specific modifier.
missing_descriptors: Subtle herbs, white flowers; dried flowers in Biser.
editor_conclusion: Add as possible rather than defining descriptors.

comparison: CEVVIN explicitly says vanilla can appear in good years; NIN repeats vanillin and spices in the finish. Other sources do not make it universal.
independence: National technical source and independent synthesis agree conditionally.
missing_definition: Vanilla may arise from fermentation, grape aroma or oak, and no cause is established here.
missing_descriptors: Conditional vanilla/vanillin and spice.
editor_conclusion: Include only with «иногда/в хорошие годы» and no oak inference.

comparison: CEVVIN directly says Smederevka is often blended to improve acidity; the technical Serbian profile repeats acid correction and improved organoleptic balance.
independence: Current national and separate technical sources converge.
missing_definition: This is a legitimate blending function, not correction of a legal defect unless the specific wine and law say so.
editor_conclusion: Add as a traditional technological use.

comparison: CEVVIN says grapes are consumed fresh to a large extent; Falstaff and technical sources independently classify frequent table-grape use.
independence: National, international specialist and technical sources converge.
missing_definition: Dual-purpose means both fresh consumption and processing, with proportions varying by country and period.
editor_conclusion: Add fresh/table-grape use to avoid a wine-only definition.

comparison: Current CEVVIN directly reports rank 12 and names South Banat, Three Moravas and Šumadija as the largest regions; English Wikipedia repeats rank and older percentages.
independence: Authoritative current register analysis with encyclopaedic secondary support.
missing_definition: Rank and regional shares require an access date and refer to registered commercial plantings.
editor_conclusion: Add the dated rank and regions, using CEVVIN rather than stale Wikipedia percentages.

comparison: CEVVIN directly states early vegetation, very late fourth-epoch ripening, strong cold sensitivity and need for favourable sunny ventilated sites; Falstaff independently agrees on late ripening and frost vulnerability.
independence: National technical and international specialist sources converge.
missing_definition: Early budbreak plus winter-frost sensitivity and late harvest create separate seasonal risks.
editor_conclusion: Add as essential agronomic context, especially when comparing regions.

comparison: The current producer page directly lists Biser as 100% Smederevka traditional-method sparkling wine; Falstaff independently catalogues and rates the 2016 release.
independence: Current primary product and independent international tasting converge.
missing_definition: The current page does not disclose dosage, vintage or lees time; do not infer Champagne-style details beyond traditional method.
editor_conclusion: Add Biser as the concrete Serbian proof of sparkling use and record it in the omissions section.

comparison: Falstaff's independent 2016 note and the current producer note overlap on liveliness, apple and bread/biscuit tones while contributing complementary fruit and finish detail.
independence: Independent tasting plus current producer description, probably different releases.
missing_definition: Lees-derived biscuit/croissant is a bottle-specific inference unless maturation data are published.
missing_descriptors: Lively mousse; white stone fruit, lime, biscuit/croissant, green or yellow apple, fresh acidity and citrus finish.
editor_conclusion: Add as Biser-specific descriptors with the 2016 Falstaff attribution and separate current producer note.

comparison: Official EU usage, CEVVIN, Serbian sources and several Wikipedias consistently map Četereška/Csetereska to Kadarka/Skadarka.
independence: Regulatory, national technical, encyclopaedic and journalistic sources converge.
missing_definition: Preserve original spellings and label Četereška as a regional synonym, not a separate clone.
editor_conclusion: Keep the synonym, preferably as «Kadarka (Četereška/Csetereska)».

comparison: CEVVIN identifies Subotica among the largest present Serbian areas and says Skadarka was formerly the leading local variety there; RTS and current producers corroborate the association.
independence: National register-derived profile and current local practice agree.
missing_definition: The card's locality is not a claim of exclusive origin; Kadarka is distributed across several Serbian and foreign regions.
editor_conclusion: Keep Subotica as the card's regional anchor, not as the cultivar's sole home.

comparison: Ruby red is explicit for the Dukay base wine and Croatian Wikipedia; professional examples range from light ruby to deeper red.
independence: Bottle-specific and multilingual sources agree on ruby as possible, while showing colour range.
missing_definition: Ruby is a hue family, not a fixed intensity measurement.
editor_conclusion: Use «often light ruby» or attribute ruby colour to the particular wine.

comparison: Spice repeats across Hungarian, German, Serbian and Croatian profiles, RTS, specialist press and the Dukay product page.
independence: Encyclopaedic, national, journalistic and bottle-specific sources converge.
missing_definition: Spice can include pepper, paprika, clove, gingerbread or a generic spicy impression; do not flatten all into one compound.
editor_conclusion: Keep spice as a core possible descriptor.

comparison: Medium body is supported by Croatian Wikipedia and particular wines, but Hungarian official communication and Serbian specialist profiles place the common range at light to medium.
independence: Multiple languages and bottles show a bounded but real stylistic range.
missing_definition: Body depends on alcohol, extract, tannin and production; it is not fixed by variety alone.
missing_descriptors: Light and light-to-medium examples are common and should be named alongside medium-bodied ones.
editor_conclusion: Change the general formula to «light to medium-bodied».

comparison: Hungarian, Serbian and Croatian descriptions and the official Hungarian portal favour pale/elegant Kadarka, whereas English and German Wikipedia explicitly allow medium-dark, dark, tannic and extract-rich wines; Dukay Reserve itself calls its deeper red unusual.
independence: The conflict spans encyclopaedic traditions and is reconciled by specialist evidence for clone, crop-load and vinification variation.
missing_definition: Separate typical modern light style from the full technical possibility range; colour should be measured rather than inferred from prose.
editor_conclusion: Keep «deep colour is atypical» only with a variability caveat and mention existing dark expressions.

comparison: Many red Kadarkas are visually pale yet marketed and made as red wine, while the same low-pigment cultivar is also popular for rosé. No objective hue threshold supports «does not fade to rosé» as a universal sensory boundary.
independence: Official Hungarian style guidance and product practice establish both red and rosé uses; the exact phrase remains rhetorical.
missing_definition: Red versus rosé is chiefly a production/category distinction involving skin contact and intended style, not merely how pale a glass appears.
editor_conclusion: Replace the metaphor with «often pale for a red; Kadarka is also widely made as rosé».

comparison: German and Russian Wikipedia directly describe thin or very thin berry skin; specialist profiles repeat the trait.
independence: Two languages and specialist literature converge.
missing_definition: Skin thickness should ideally be an OIV-measured cultivar trait; casual visual assessment is less precise.
editor_conclusion: Keep thin skin as an ampelographic characteristic.

comparison: Thin skin and pale wine co-occur in several descriptions, but the official Hungarian explanation points to low anthocyanins and a Kadarka fermentation experiment shows colour changes with maceration and temperature. No controlled evidence isolates skin thinness as the cause.
independence: Ampelography, official sensory guidance and cultivar-specific enology cover different links in the causal chain.
missing_definition: Wine colour depends on pigment concentration and composition, skin-to-juice ratio, extraction, pH, oxygen and ageing, not skin thickness alone.
editor_conclusion: Remove «отсюда» or replace it with «light colour reflects low pigment supply and extraction; thin skin may contribute but is not a sufficient explanation».

comparison: CEVVIN, German Wikipedia, Hungarian specialist material and Serbian wine press consistently call Kadarka highly susceptible to grey mould/Botrytis.
independence: National technical, encyclopaedic and specialist sources converge.
missing_definition: Grey mould/grey rot in grapes is disease caused by Botrytis cinerea; in this context it is destructive bunch rot, not automatically noble rot.
editor_conclusion: Keep the susceptibility claim and define the pathogen on first use.

comparison: Thin skin plausibly contributes to damage, but CEVVIN also identifies compact bunches and a peer-reviewed review shows compactness is a major Botrytis risk; rain and site management further affect outcomes.
independence: Cultivar-specific national observations and general peer-reviewed mechanism agree on multifactor risk.
missing_definition: A causal attribution needs berry mechanical resistance, bunch compactness, microclimate and infection data.
editor_conclusion: Write «thin skin and compact bunches contribute to high Botrytis susceptibility», not a single-cause statement.

comparison: Raspberry recurs in RTS, Serbian specialist prose, Dukay base wine and independent tastings of Serbian Kadarka.
independence: General profile, local reporting, producer and professional bottle observations agree.
editor_conclusion: Keep raspberry as a well-supported possible descriptor.

comparison: Currant/red currant is explicit in Dukay and several Hungarian or professional Kadarka notes, including Serbian bottles.
independence: Producer, official Hungarian and independent tasting material converge on the descriptor family.
missing_definition: Where a source says generic currant, do not silently narrow it to red currant without colour evidence.
editor_conclusion: Keep red currant as possible, while preserving generic currant wording where applicable.

comparison: Plum appears in Dukay's base wine, Serbian specialist prose and some oak-aged Hungarian examples, but cherry and raspberry/red berry families recur more broadly.
independence: Several bottle and general sources support occurrence, with weaker frequency consensus.
missing_definition: Fresh plum, dried plum and plum preserve imply different ripeness and development.
missing_descriptors: Cherry/sour cherry, strawberry, cranberry, pepper/paprika and herbs are at least as important in the wider profile.
editor_conclusion: Keep plum as an occasional descriptor, not a mandatory core note.

comparison: The apparent source, Dukay Kadarka Reserve 2020, says Hungarian csipkebogyó, which means rosehip. It does not say wild-rose flower, and one oak-aged wine cannot establish a class-wide oak descriptor.
independence: The primary Hungarian product wording resolves the translation directly; no comparable broad source supports wild rose as an oak rule.
missing_definition: Rosehip is the fruit of a rose; wild rose usually suggests the flower aroma. They are not interchangeable tasting terms.
missing_descriptors: For the named Reserve: rosehip, cherry, spice, rounded acidity and creamy fruit.
editor_conclusion: Correct «дикая роза» to «шиповник» and attribute it specifically to Dukay Kadarka Reserve 2020.

comparison: Cherry is explicit in oak-aged Dukay Reserve and ubiquitous in non-oak and differently aged Kadarka profiles, so its occurrence is sound but its attachment to barrel ageing is causal overreach.
independence: Primary product and broad independent cultivar corpus agree on cherry across technologies.
missing_definition: Oak maturation may reshape fruit expression but does not prove that the cherry note originates from oak.
editor_conclusion: Keep cherry as a core Kadarka descriptor; cite the Reserve only as a specific example.

comparison: German Wikipedia and concentrated examples allow substantial tannin, but Hungarian official guidance, Croatian Wikipedia and many modern bottles describe restrained, soft or delicate tannins.
independence: The cross-language disagreement reflects genuine style variation rather than a simple factual error.
missing_definition: Report extraction, crop load, clone and ageing before generalizing tannin intensity.
editor_conclusion: Use «usually restrained, but can be noticeable in concentrated versions».

comparison: Fresh or firm acidity repeats in Hungarian official guidance, RTS, specialist press, Dukay and professional tastings; measured wines also show substantial but variable values.
independence: National, producer and independent tasting evidence converge.
missing_definition: Sensory acidity and titratable acidity are related but not identical; retain units and method if numbers are added.
editor_conclusion: Keep noticeable/fresh acidity as a common characteristic.

comparison: German Wikipedia says successful dark Kadarka ages well, Serbian specialist prose allows complex examples beyond a decade, while official Hungarian guidance recommends the light style within one or two years because it oxidizes relatively quickly. No source establishes exactly two to three years for all styles.
independence: Encyclopaedic, national and specialist sources describe different wine styles and therefore different drinking windows.
missing_definition: Ageing potential must be attached to producer, vintage, extraction, closure and storage; «benefit» requires a sensory trajectory.
editor_conclusion: Replace the fixed rule with separate early-drinking and structured-ageworthy styles; date individual recommendations by wine.

comparison: The public wein.plus entry reports around 150 synonyms, and its general synonym article explicitly includes Kadarka among cultivars with more than one hundred names.
independence: This is a specialist catalogue assertion; exact counts vary with whether spelling variants, erroneous names and distinct genotypes are included.
missing_definition: Name the catalogue and accessed date; distinguish accepted synonyms from historic misspellings and misidentifications.
editor_conclusion: Keep «more than one hundred», attribute the approximate 150 count to public wein.plus rather than an unspecified international catalogue.

comparison: Gamza is consistently mapped to Kadarka in the EU list, EN/RU/DE Wikipedias, CEVVIN, wein.plus, RTS and ASI.
independence: Official, technical and multilingual sources converge.
missing_definition: Gamza is especially the Bulgarian name; commercial usage elsewhere may vary.
editor_conclusion: Keep Gamza as a documented synonym.

comparison: Četereška/Csetereska is confirmed by EU usage, CEVVIN, Russian/German Wikipedia and Serbian sources.
independence: Regulatory, technical and local sources agree.
missing_definition: Retain transliteration and diacritics; do not confuse the synonym with a separately certified clone unless a clone record is supplied.
editor_conclusion: Keep the synonym with one Latin spelling at first mention.

comparison: Braničevka/Branicevka is listed by CEVVIN, public wein.plus, RTS and ASI as a Kadarka name.
independence: National technical, specialist and international professional sources converge, though some may share the same ampelographic tradition.
missing_definition: Country assignment differs between catalogues; synonym identity is stronger than the precise national label.
editor_conclusion: Keep Braničevka as a documented synonym.

comparison: Popular wine narratives can make Prokupac an indirect ancestor by combining Papazkarasi = Alba Imputotato × Prokupac with a proposed Papazkarasi × Skardarsko origin of Kadarka. Current genetics does not establish direct Prokupac–Kadarka parentage and gives Kadarka a first-degree Heunisch Weiss relationship.
independence: The indirect claim is a composite of older/popular pedigree summaries; the newer peer-reviewed Serbian study is stronger for tested accessions.
missing_definition: Ancestor, parent and broader relative are different genetic claims. State the accession and study before drawing a pedigree.
editor_conclusion: Do not say simply that Prokupac is Kadarka's ancestor; explain it only as an unresolved indirect hypothesis.

comparison: The 2024 peer-reviewed study indeed finds extensive Balkan family structure and treats Prokupac as a major lineage founder, but it does not connect it directly to Kadarka; Kadarka SRB is parent–offspring related to Heunisch Weiss.
independence: Current multilocus genetics has priority over unsourced historical pedigrees; Wikipedia does not adequately capture the newer result.
missing_definition: A genetic cluster or shared regional network is not proof of direct descent.
editor_conclusion: Keep the caution and add the specific Heunisch Weiss first-degree result instead of the vague phrase alone.

comparison: Multiple Serbian and Hungarian narratives link Kadarka's northward spread to Serbs displaced by Ottoman wars and the Great Migration around 1690, but CEVVIN explicitly dates movement into the Pannonian plain to the eighteenth century. The exact seventeenth-century formulation is therefore not settled.
independence: Producer and promotional histories are not archival; the national technical source conflicts on century and also lacks an explicit archival citation.
missing_definition: Distinguish first introduction, wider spread and later replanting; «Great Migration» commonly refers to the 1690 event but movement continued afterward.
editor_conclusion: Write «probably spread north with Serb migrations under Ottoman pressure in the late seventeenth to eighteenth centuries» unless an archival cultivar record fixes the date.

comparison: The official Hungarian portal explicitly says Kadarka is not Hungarian in origin yet is now considered Hungarian and at home in the Carpathian Basin. This confirms cultural adoption but not the book's unmeasurable equality «с не меньшим основанием».
independence: Hungarian self-description is primary for current cultural framing; origin remains separately disputed in multilingual sources.
missing_definition: Cultural identity, historical importance and genetic/geographic origin are distinct questions.
editor_conclusion: Replace the parity judgement with the attributable statement that Hungary treats Kadarka as a local/national heritage variety despite non-Hungarian origin.

comparison: The 2019 CEVVIN inventory directly reports 11.60 ha of Kadarka in Serbia's commercial vineyards.
independence: This is the authoritative national specialist figure; the six Wikipedias and public wein.plus do not independently reproduce it.
missing_definition: Keep the year and denominator «registered commercial vineyards»; it excludes unregistered household vines and is not a 2026 current-area estimate.
editor_conclusion: Keep 11.60 ha with explicit CEVVIN 2019 attribution and scope.

comparison: 11.60 ha is objectively a tiny national commercial area and CEVVIN ranks the cultivar low, but «совсем мало» should remain tied to that 2019 registered denominator.
independence: National inventory supplies the quantitative base; journalistic and producer sources concur qualitatively.
missing_definition: Comparative rarity should state a denominator or ranking rather than rely only on an adjective.
editor_conclusion: Write «only 11.60 registered commercial hectares in the 2019 CEVVIN inventory».

comparison: The 2022 specialist snapshot practically found Tonković, Sagmeister and Maurer, and all three remain visible. Current SerbianWine.rs and menus suggest additional or ambiguous names such as Brindza and Čuvardić, so three is not a complete timeless count.
independence: Current producer and tasting records confirm the core trio; evidence for extra bottlers is weaker or inconsistent.
missing_definition: Define whether «market» means nationally distributed bottled wine, cellar sales, restaurant table wine or any labelled release, and date the search.
editor_conclusion: Retain «few», date the three-name list to the 2022 article and avoid presenting it as exhaustive today.

comparison: Tonković's current primary catalogue remains entirely centred on Kadarka and spans white blanc de noirs, rosé and multiple red styles.
independence: Producer evidence is direct and the winery's market prominence is independently reported.
missing_descriptors: The book elsewhere omits named current labels Allegro, Fantazija, Rapsodija and Rosé; these are already recorded in G0094–G0097.
editor_conclusion: Keep Tonković among the principal current bottlers.

comparison: Current importer sheets, Falstaff and Serbian wine press document several Sagmeister vineyard-designated Kadarka releases.
independence: Commercial and independent professional tasting sources converge.
missing_definition: Producer ownership and labels changed after the Dukay–Sagmeister partnership; date individual wines and owners.
editor_conclusion: Keep Sagmeister among the principal bottlers, with current versus historical labels separated.

comparison: SerbianWine.rs, importer records and Falstaff document Maurer Kadarka 1880, Gravitation and other Kadarka releases from northern Serbian sites.
independence: User-requested guide, current commercial sheets and independent tasting records agree.
missing_definition: Maurer's Subotica and Fruška Gora sites should not be merged into one terroir.
editor_conclusion: Keep Maurer among the principal bottlers.

comparison: Modern Serbian sources consistently describe Kadarka as formerly dominant on Fruška Gora, but the checked corpus lacks a primary historical vineyard census with cultivar denominator.
independence: The two main Serbian reports may share producer memory and secondary histories; they are not independent archival measurements.
missing_definition: «Главный красный» could mean largest area among red cultivars or majority of all vineyard area; the source must specify which.
editor_conclusion: Use «reported as historically dominant» unless a dated census or agricultural survey is found.

comparison: Vino.rs states about 60% of Fruška Gora vineyard area roughly a century ago, but supplies no primary citation. Similar 60% figures circulate for all Hungarian vineyards, creating a real risk of denominator transfer.
independence: The positive evidence is one modern Serbian article; Hungarian parallels are contextual, not independent confirmation of Fruška Gora.
missing_definition: Need year, geographic boundary, all-vineyard versus red-variety denominator and the original survey table.
editor_conclusion: Keep only as «vino.rs reports about 60%» and flag it for archival verification.

comparison: The 2021 interview directly quotes Sagmeister saying Kadarka made up two thirds of Fruška Gora vineyard plantings in the nineteenth century.
independence: The quotation is primary evidence of his statement but not independent evidence that the historical statistic is true.
missing_definition: Specify which nineteenth-century year or period and denominator; none is supplied in the interview.
editor_conclusion: Keep strictly attributed to Sagmeister, not as a verified census result.

comparison: The 60% and 66.7% formulations are numerically compatible, but the source trail shows one specialist article and one producer quotation without archival tables; treating them as two confirmations would overstate independence.
independence: Both belong to a small modern Serbian wine-media network and may draw from the same oral or secondary tradition.
missing_definition: Source independence requires distinct underlying documents, not merely two webpages.
editor_conclusion: Present them as two modern formulations of one unverified historical tradition.

comparison: Serbian and Hungarian specialist histories agree that socialist planned production and vineyard restructuring sharply reduced Kadarka after World War II.
independence: Different national histories converge on the same industrial-policy mechanism, though Serbian losses are not quantified here.
missing_definition: Separate the multinational Yugoslav period from Hungarian communism and date Serbia-specific restructuring where possible.
editor_conclusion: Keep the Yugoslav-era decline as a supported broad history, adding dates if a Serbian planting series is found.

comparison: More productive and economically reliable cultivars, including international ones, displaced Kadarka, but sources also stress mechanization, uneven ripening, rot/frost risk and labour intensity. «Higher yield» alone is incomplete.
independence: Serbian reporting and Hungarian wine history converge on a multifactor industrial-production explanation.
missing_definition: Distinguish biological yield, regularity, machine suitability and processing economics.
editor_conclusion: Expand the cause to «more productive, regular and mechanization-friendly cultivars under mass-production policy».

comparison: The 1816 Skadarka mention is well supported as an early Serbian ampelographic record, but neither the academic synthesis nor the visible book catalogue establishes that it was the first written trace. Older Kadarka/Cadarca records exist elsewhere in the eighteenth century.
independence: Multiple sources confirm the book and mention, while the priority superlative lacks a primary comparative bibliography.
missing_definition: «First» must specify world, Serbia, Srem or Fruška Gora and whether it means any name occurrence or a full ampelographic description.
editor_conclusion: Replace «first written trace» with «an important early Serbian written description/mention in 1816».

comparison: Bibliographic records and modern scholarship agree that Prokopije Bolić published Soveršen vinodelac in Buda in 1816 as an early Serbian viticulture and winemaking manual.
independence: Physical-edition metadata and scholarly citation converge.
missing_definition: Transliteration varies: Soveršen vinodelac / Совершен виноделац; preserve the historical title rather than modernizing silently.
editor_conclusion: Keep author, title, place and year.

comparison: The historical-book listing and biographical references identify Bolić as archimandrite of Rakovac Monastery on Fruška Gora.
independence: Bibliographic and ecclesiastical-biographical evidence agree.
editor_conclusion: Keep the title and monastery affiliation.

comparison: The 2024 peer-reviewed paper confirms Skadarka/Kadarka Kek in Bolić's 1816 cultivar discussion, and the ampelography history says the manual described 35 Srem cultivars. The exact superlative «among the most important» is not visible in the checked primary text.
independence: Scholarly synthesis and bibliographic history confirm inclusion; ranking remains unverified.
missing_definition: Separate presence in a cultivar list from an explicit priority or acreage rank.
editor_conclusion: Write «Bolić included Skadarka among the Fruška Gora/Srem cultivars he described», omitting «most important» until the page is checked.

comparison: Official EU terminology, CEVVIN, wein.plus, EN/DE/RU Wikipedia and Wine Grapes all treat Kadarka, Skadarka and Četereška/Cetereska as names of one cultivar.
independence: Regulatory, national viticulture, specialist reference and multilingual encyclopedia sources converge.
missing_definition: Normalize Četereška/Cetereska/Csetereska as spelling variants while preserving the source form.
editor_conclusion: Keep the one-cultivar statement.

comparison: Kadarka is plainly the established Hungarian and international form, and sources describe the cultivar's transfer into Hungary. They do not demonstrate that the lexeme originated in Hungarian; one major hypothesis instead relates it to Skadar/Scutari through Slavic usage.
independence: Hungarian official communication, Hungarian Wikipedia and Wine Grapes agree on Hungarian usage but not on a Hungarian etymological origin.
missing_definition: Distinguish «name used in Hungarian wine culture» from «word coined or etymologically derived in Hungarian».
editor_conclusion: Write «Kadarka became the usual Hungarian form» rather than implying proven Hungarian word origin.

comparison: Četereška is demonstrably used in Negotinska Krajina, including the current Bukovski Cuvée composition, and local sources associate the synonym with Serbian Kadarka. Official and international lists also use Cetereska more broadly, so «local» should not mean «exclusive».
independence: Current product data, Serbian reporting, CEVVIN and official synonymy converge on real regional usage.
missing_definition: State whether «local name» means locally current, historically recorded or legally official; it is not exclusive to Negotin.
editor_conclusion: Keep the Negotin association but add «one of the local names» or omit exclusivity.

comparison: The link of Skadarka/Kadarka to Skadar, Shkodër or Lake Scutari is widespread in Hungarian Wikipedia, Wine Grapes, EN Wikipedia and producer histories, but it is an etymological tradition rather than demonstrated historical linguistics.
independence: Several source families repeat the link, though some likely derive from the same older ampelographic literature.
missing_definition: Separate Skadar city, Lake Skadar/Scutari and the distinct cultivar name Skadarsko; sources sometimes conflate them.
editor_conclusion: Keep only as «one hypothesis links the name with Skadar/Shkodër».

comparison: High-quality specialist and official Hungarian sources explicitly frame the Skadar association and migration pathway as uncertain, and current genetics does not establish a geographic birthplace from the name.
independence: Wine Grapes, official Hungarian communication and conflicting Wikipedias independently require caution.
missing_definition: Etymology, migration history and genetic origin are separate questions and must not be treated as mutual proof.
editor_conclusion: Keep the explicit hypothesis warning.

comparison: The exact origin is unresolved. The checked corpus advances mutually incompatible Skadar/Albanian, Bulgarian, Romanian, Hungarian, North Macedonian and Asia Minor stories, while the strongest synthesis limits the conclusion to a broad Balkan–Pannonian area.
independence: Official, specialist and six-language Wikipedia evidence shows genuine disagreement rather than one settled origin.
missing_definition: Use «exact geographic origin» and avoid equating current cultural ownership with botanical origin.
editor_conclusion: Keep «origin remains disputed», optionally adding «probably Balkan–Pannonian».

comparison: Kadarka is directly visible in current bottling names, Skadarka is documented in Bolić and later Serbian cultivation, and Četereška is present in official lists and a current Negotin blend description. The audit did not find a controlled label corpus proving that each of the three independently appears as a front-label cultivar name.
independence: Historical literature, current producer pages and product records demonstrate real usage, but not the book's exact universal label formulation.
missing_definition: Distinguish a historical assortment/list, back-label blend composition, product catalogue and front-label varietal name.
editor_conclusion: Change to «all three occur in historical and current wine usage» unless label images for each form are supplied.

comparison: Serbian institutional profiles explicitly define Začinak and Župski Bojadiser primarily by colour-correction roles and Tamjanika partly by aroma correction. Yet these grapes can produce wine themselves, and Vranac/Tamjanika are commonly planted for varietal bottlings.
independence: CEVVIN, the breeding university, vocational literature and current producers converge on helper roles without exclusivity.
missing_definition: Replace «not for their own wine» with «often or primarily used as blending components» and distinguish planting intent from cellar use.
editor_conclusion: Keep the helper-grape concept but remove the absolute formulation.

comparison: CEVVIN directly classifies Začinak among teinturier-type cultivars, describes very dark wine and says it is mainly used to correct other wines' colour; older vocational literature and current Bukovski Cuvée practice agree.
independence: National viticulture profile, historical manual and current product evidence converge.
missing_definition: Začinak's must is semi-coloured, so avoid implying it is identical in pigment anatomy to every classic teinturier.
editor_conclusion: Keep the colour-helper role.

comparison: The breeding institution and CEVVIN both state that Župski Bojadiser has intensely coloured juice/wine and is used primarily to increase red-wine colour intensity.
independence: Primary breeder and national viticulture centre independently agree, with a current Župa blend example.
missing_definition: It is a 1979 recognized Serbian bred cultivar, not an ancient traditional variety.
editor_conclusion: Keep the colour role and define it as a teinturier cross.

comparison: Academy-backed Vranac material, EN/DE Wikipedia and Decanter consistently describe deeply or intensely coloured grapes and wine; current blends show it can contribute this trait.
independence: Academic lexicon synthesis, encyclopedias and competition-oriented specialist press converge.
editor_conclusion: Keep «depth of colour» as a typical potential contribution, not a guaranteed blending outcome.

comparison: Vranac is consistently full-bodied, extractive and tannic, so it can contribute body and structure. «Density» is understandable sensory shorthand but not a single measured attribute.
independence: CANU-backed description, Decanter and producer wines agree.
missing_definition: Define density through body, dry extract, phenolics/tannin and alcohol rather than treating it as one analytical value.
editor_conclusion: Prefer «body and structure» to «density».

comparison: No checked authoritative source describes Kavčina as a bouquet enhancer. Sources identifying it with Modra Kavčina/Žametovka describe light colour, high acidity or neutral/simple blend wine; wein.plus additionally warns that Kavčina Crna identity is ambiguous.
independence: Historical vocational, Slovenian official and specialist lexicon evidence all fail to support the proposed aromatic role and instead point elsewhere.
missing_definition: Specify which accession/name Kavčina denotes and provide a historical Serbian source for the claimed bouquet role; bouquet itself can mean mature tertiary aroma or total nose.
missing_descriptors: No characteristic primary aromatic profile supporting a bouquet-correction function was found.
editor_conclusion: Remove «Kavčina for bouquet» unless a precise historical source and cultivar identity are supplied; likely describe it instead as a light/high-acid blend grape.

comparison: CEVVIN explicitly says Tamjanika may improve other wines' taste and smell, and a current Župa wine blends it with Italian Riesling. The evidence supports aromatic blending but not a rule that the partner must always be neutral.
independence: National cultivar profile, regional producer example, SerbianWine.rs and multilingual Muscat references converge.
missing_definition: Use «less aromatic/neutral varieties» as a common application, not a mandatory pairing category.
missing_descriptors: Muscat, floral, citrus, grape, herbs and ripe fruit are the relevant aroma family; exact notes vary by wine.
editor_conclusion: Keep the aroma-helper role with «can be blended» rather than a universal practice.

comparison: Current and historical evidence shows the same cultivars used in blends, field co-ferments and varietal wines. Začinak and Župski Bojadiser have principal helper functions but not a legal or biological prohibition on standalone wine.
independence: Institutional profiles and multiple current commercial formats converge.
editor_conclusion: Keep the non-rigid-role warning.

comparison: Vranac is typically produced varietally, including numerous current 100% and dominant-Vranac commercial wines, while also being suitable for blends.
independence: CANU-backed encyclopedia material, Decanter results and winery portfolios agree.
editor_conclusion: Keep Vranac as a standalone/base-wine example.

comparison: CEVVIN describes ordinary and dessert Tamjanika wine, SerbianWine.rs documents dry, sparkling and late-harvest interpretations, and numerous current producers bottle it as a named varietal.
independence: National viticulture profile, public wine guide and current winery records converge.
editor_conclusion: Keep Tamjanika as a standalone varietal example.

comparison: Mixed-variety old vineyards and current Negotin field-blend co-ferments are directly documented, and their components deliver complementary colour, aroma, acidity and body. The metaphor that every old vineyard was intentionally assembled as a palette is plausible but not directly proven as a universal historical design principle.
independence: Current physical mixed vineyards, producer technical records and cultivar-function sources support the mechanism; archival intent evidence is limited.
missing_definition: Distinguish mixed planting, field blend, joint harvest/co-fermentation and later cellar blending; they are not interchangeable.
editor_conclusion: Write «mixed plantings could function as a palette of complementary traits» rather than stating one universal old logic.

comparison: Frontiers, VIVC-derived records, German Wikipedia, CEVVIN and wein.plus converge on Plovdina/Slankamenka Crvena/Pamid identity. Wein.plus separately treats unqualified white Slankamenka as another cultivar, so the compressed heading is safe only with «Crvena» retained.
independence: Peer-reviewed genotyping, national viticulture inventory, international catalogue tradition and specialist lexicon converge, while also exposing a real name collision.
missing_definition: Always distinguish Slankamenka Crvena/Pamid from Slankamenka Bela/white Slankamenka and from the broader CEVVIN group label.
editor_conclusion: Keep Plovdina = Pamid and Slankamenka Crvena = Pamid, but never shorten the latter to bare Slankamenka.

comparison: CEVVIN calls it a very old Balkan cultivar, Frontiers says Plovdina/Pamid is considered cultivated in Serbia for centuries, and Wikipedias call it old. The stronger ancient-Thracian continuity story is repeated but poorly sourced and cannot be dated by the genetic survey.
independence: Institutional, scholarly and encyclopedia sources agree on great age; only the exact ancient chronology lacks robust independent proof.
missing_definition: Separate «very old traditional Balkan cultivar» from continuous cultivation since a named ancient people or period.
editor_conclusion: Use «very old traditional Balkan red cultivar»; do not state Thracian continuity as established fact.

comparison: Frontiers and the Wikipedias identify Pamid with Bulgaria, while German Wikipedia and wein.plus place origin in the Bulgaria–Greece border zone. «Bulgarian» is sound cultural/catalogue attribution, not proof of an exclusive modern-state birthplace.
independence: Genetic research, large encyclopedias and a specialist lexicon converge on Bulgarian association but vary in geographic precision.
missing_definition: Distinguish VIVC country attribution, current cultural association and demonstrated geographic origin.
editor_conclusion: Keep «Bulgarian-associated Pamid» or «Pamid, catalogued as Bulgarian», adding that exact origin is placed near the Bulgaria–Greece border.

comparison: VIVC 8899's catalogue-derived synonym set, German Wikipedia, CEVVIN and wein.plus all map Crvena Slankamenka/Slankamenka Crvena and Plovdina to Pamid.
independence: International-catalogue, national-institutional and specialist sources converge; German Wikipedia partly reproduces VIVC, so it is corroboration rather than fully independent evidence.
missing_definition: Normalize word order and diacritics but preserve the source form; a synonym is a name mapping, not evidence that every accession so called is genetically identical.
editor_conclusion: Keep the VIVC synonym statement with passport number 8899.

comparison: JKI confirms that VIVC is an international scientifically curated grapevine catalogue with passport, description, image, bibliography and genetic-profile data. It does not promise literally every vernacular name for every individual vine.
independence: The official maintainer description is controlling; Wikipedia and research-paper usage are secondary confirmation.
missing_definition: VIVC records cultivar identities and accessions, including curated synonyms, homonyms and misnomers; «each vine» is misleading.
editor_conclusion: Define VIVC as an international cultivar and genetic-resource catalogue that consolidates accepted names and synonyms.

comparison: The Leposavić/Banjska identification appears only in the winery's own history. The independent 2024 survey proves that Pamid was frequently found in old Serbian vineyards, but its visible site data do not link those 29 samples to Lakićević or Leposavić.
independence: The site-specific assertion lacks an independent lab report; national evidence cannot be substituted for a named location.
missing_definition: Publish the sampling site, accession code, laboratory, marker panel and match report, and distinguish old vineyard land from an individual surviving vine.
editor_conclusion: Attribute the Leposavić result explicitly to Vinarija Lakićević until a laboratory or supplementary record links the accession to that site.

comparison: The current Serbian CEVVIN page says «Slankamenka (Grupa Plovina)», not «группа Пловдина». Plovdina is one of the names inside that category.
independence: This is a direct comparison with the named Serbian catalogue, so the catalogue's own wording is decisive.
missing_definition: Plovina and Plovdina are not interchangeable spellings in a quoted category name.
editor_conclusion: Correct the audit note to «CEVVIN group Plovina» while leaving the book text unchanged.

comparison: CEVVIN directly reports 22nd place by represented area in commercial plantings. The page does not make this a timeless national rank across all private and abandoned vines.
independence: The claim derives from the named centre's own survey; no independent recent national acreage table was found, but the quotation is exact.
missing_definition: State commercial vineyards and, if available later, add survey year and hectares.
editor_conclusion: Keep rank 22 with «according to CEVVIN's commercial-planting survey».

comparison: CEVVIN says thin and lower in alcohol; English, German and Russian Wikipedias independently describe light, low-extract or pale young wine.
independence: National technical description and three-language encyclopedia profiles converge, though the Wikipedia pages share some source lineage.
missing_definition: Light body, low extract and low alcohol are related but not identical; preserve CEVVIN's separate terms.
editor_conclusion: Keep light and relatively low-alcohol as typical style descriptors.

comparison: CEVVIN explicitly says neutral and simple. The requested Wikipedias do not provide contrary aromatic descriptors, but most only describe structure and acidity.
independence: One high-value Serbian institutional source supplies the exact term; encyclopedias are silent rather than independently confirmatory.
missing_definition: Neutral means low varietal aroma intensity, not absence of all smell or flavour.
missing_descriptors: No stable fruit, floral or spice consensus appears in the checked encyclopedias; neutral/simple is the only direct institutional profile.
editor_conclusion: Keep «neutral», preferably glossed as restrained varietal aroma.

comparison: CEVVIN directly says the wine very often has a slight reddish shade, especially from black-berried variants; German Wikipedia's pale-colour wording is compatible rather than contradictory.
independence: Serbian institutional and German encyclopedia evidence converge on a lightly coloured red/rosy appearance.
missing_definition: A reddish tint describes wine appearance and should not be confused with berry skin colour or a formal rosé production category.
editor_conclusion: Keep the slight reddish-hue descriptor as typical, not universal.

comparison: VIVC-derived/CEVVIN records use Drenak for Pamid, while Frontiers and wein.plus use it for Parmak Cerven. The book correctly warns of ambiguity, but «not a third name of the same cultivar» is too absolute because Drenak is genuinely registered as a Pamid synonym in some traditions.
independence: Peer-reviewed genetics, national catalogue and a specialist lexicon independently expose the homonym collision.
missing_definition: A synonym maps one local name to a genotype in a given source; a homonym is the same name applied to different genotypes across sources or places.
editor_conclusion: Write «Drenak is not a unique identifier: it can denote Pamid or Parmak Cerven depending on the accession and locality».

comparison: The Pamid synonym tradition reproduced from VIVC by German Wikipedia and independently repeated by CEVVIN and wein.plus includes Drenak.
independence: The sources converge but are partly dependent on VIVC; the point is still a direct catalogue-name fact.
missing_definition: Catalogue inclusion does not override a conflicting homonym in another cultivar passport or regional usage.
editor_conclusion: Keep «VIVC lists Drenak under Pamid», immediately followed by the homonym warning.

comparison: Frontiers genotyped one old Serbian vine as Parmak Cerven and explicitly states Drenak is a Parmak Cerven synonym. The visible main article does not show that this exact accession was originally collected under the field name Drenak; that link is said to reside in Supplementary Material 1.
independence: Peer-reviewed genotyping establishes the cultivar and synonym relation, while wein.plus independently confirms Drenak under Parmak Cerven; the exact sample-label chain remains unverified in the main text.
missing_definition: Cite the supplementary accession row or avoid claiming the sampled plant itself bore the Drenak field label.
editor_conclusion: Use «the study identified one old Serbian vine as Parmak Cerven and treats Drenak as its synonym» unless the supplementary row is attached.

comparison: Because two distinct genotypes share Drenak in authoritative and specialist records, name-only identification is unsafe. JKI explicitly documents synonym, homonym and misnomer corrections through genetic fingerprints plus morphology.
independence: Official identity-method guidance, peer-reviewed genotyping and cross-database homonym evidence converge.
missing_definition: Analysis should mean accession-level ampelography and preferably SSR/SNP comparison, not a chemical test of finished wine.
editor_conclusion: Keep the warning and specify morphological/genetic identification of the vine sample.

comparison: VIVC-derived identity, all six requested Wikipedias and specialist references converge that Grašac/Graševina, Italian Riesling/Riesling Italico and Welschriesling denote the same cultivar, separate from Rhine Riesling.
independence: International registry tradition, multilingual encyclopedias and peer-reviewed genetic literature agree.
missing_definition: Grašac is the Serbian market/historical form; Graševina is especially Croatian; spelling and national usage should not be flattened into one preferred label everywhere.
editor_conclusion: Keep the three-way synonymy and, where useful, add that it is unrelated to Rhine Riesling.

comparison: The 2025 register still gives Grašac 8% of commercial vineyard area, while older tables placed it first among whites; broad producer presence and its bulk-to-premium range support the workhorse metaphor. It is not an official technical classification.
independence: Official area data, specialist synthesis, wein.plus and Serbian winery directories converge on scale and flexibility.
missing_definition: Workhorse should mean widely planted, reliable and used across substantial everyday production, not intrinsically low quality.
editor_conclusion: Keep as an attributed industry metaphor or write «one of Serbia's principal workhorse white grapes».

comparison: Older sources and the public wein.plus table support Grašac as Serbia's leading white, explaining the wording. The official end-2025 Vineyard Register now places Chardonnay at 9% and Grašac at 8%, so the unqualified present-tense superlative is obsolete for predominantly commercial registered vineyards.
independence: The current Ministry register is more recent and methodologically explicit than Wikipedia, producer pages and older secondary tables.
missing_definition: Always give year, register coverage and whether the ranking includes table grapes, household plots and unregistered vines.
editor_conclusion: For 2025 write «Serbia's second most planted white cultivar in the commercial register, behind Chardonnay; formerly listed first in older tables».

comparison: The cultivar is distributed across many Central and Southeastern European countries and is not genetically proven Serbian. Yet SerbianWine.rs calls it a historic regional white and Croatian tradition often treats Graševina as domesticated/autochthonous, showing that «international» and «regional» are editorial taxonomies rather than a single formal status.
independence: Multilingual encyclopedias, VIVC identity and regional guides converge on cross-border distribution while differing in cultural classification.
missing_definition: Separate international distribution, regional domestication, autochthonous genetic origin and the book's chapter placement.
editor_conclusion: Call it an internationally distributed Central European cultivar with a long Serbian regional tradition, not simply «formally international».

comparison: A genuine 1812–1824 Graschaz herbarium record makes Sremski Karlovci an important early documented centre and a plausible candidate. The 2020 genetic study finds one northern-Italian parent but leaves the crossing site unresolved; German/Hungarian Wikipedias lean Italy or France, while other traditions favour the Danube basin.
independence: Archival naming evidence and genetic genealogy are independent but answer different questions; neither proves a Karlovci birthplace.
missing_definition: The earliest currently known specimen/name record is not automatically the place where the genotype originated.
editor_conclusion: Write «Sremski Karlovci is one proposed origin and an early documented centre»; do not rank it as established birthplace.

comparison: The Karlovci herbarium, two centuries of Srem usage, older leading acreage and extensive current winery presence make Grašac culturally and agriculturally at home in Serbia regardless of unresolved genetic origin.
independence: Archival, official statistical, specialist and current portfolio evidence converge on long local establishment.
missing_definition: «Domestic» here means long naturalized/regional cultivation and cultural ownership, not legal autochthony or demonstrated birthplace.
editor_conclusion: Keep the cultural-domestication statement, explicitly separating it from the origin hypothesis.

comparison: Traminac is established Serbian usage, but Croatian Wikipedia and international synonym lists show the same form across the South Slavic wine area. It can label several members/forms of the Traminer family.
independence: Multilingual encyclopedias and specialist nomenclature converge on regional use and ambiguity.
missing_definition: Distinguish a linguistic regional name from the registered cultivar identity on a specific wine or vineyard accession.
editor_conclusion: Write «Serbian and Croatian regional name for Traminer-family grapes, often the aromatic form».

comparison: Wein.plus calls Gewürztraminer by far the most common Traminer and EN/DE sources support Traminac Mirisavi mapping to it. Yet actual Srem records also use Traminac Beli, and the family has unstable/misapplied names, so «most cases» is plausible but not quantified for Serbian labels.
independence: Specialist taxonomy and independent wine records agree on Gewürz prominence while directly showing other label forms.
missing_definition: For each wine record the registered grape should be checked as Gewürztraminer/Traminac Mirisavi, Traminac Beli, Traminac Crveni or another accession.
editor_conclusion: Keep «usually Gewürztraminer» only with the warning that bare Traminac is not genetically decisive.

comparison: Rose is repeated across EN, DE, RU, HR, Decanter, German official regional material and independent Srem tastings.
independence: Multilingual encyclopedias, specialist reference and actual-wine tasting notes converge.
missing_descriptors: Rose petal, rose water and broader perfumed floral impressions are related but not identical vocabulary.
editor_conclusion: Keep rose as a canonical descriptor.

comparison: Lychee is the most consistent fruit marker across English Wikipedia, Decanter, other professional profiles and a 93-point Fruška Gora tasting; the shared aroma-compound research gives chemical plausibility.
independence: Encyclopedic, professional sensory and scientific-aroma lines converge.
missing_descriptors: Common companions include tropical fruit, peach, apricot, passion fruit, grapefruit and candied citrus.
editor_conclusion: Keep lychee as a canonical descriptor.

comparison: General spice is universal in the reference set, and ginger is repeatedly named by major wine guides alongside cinnamon, clove, pepper or lemongrass. Specific spices vary by wine.
independence: The name etymology, multilingual profiles and major wine press converge.
missing_definition: Use a family descriptor plus examples rather than implying every bottle smells of ginger.
missing_descriptors: Cinnamon, clove, white pepper, lemongrass and candied citrus broaden the spice/citrus range.
editor_conclusion: Keep «spice, sometimes ginger».

comparison: Vin de France, major guides and encyclopedias consistently describe Gewürztraminer as rich and relatively full-bodied, often with high alcohol. Some independently tasted Srem wines are elegant or taut rather than uniformly heavy.
independence: Official national wine profile, specialist guides and current wine tastings converge on the typical structure with exceptions.
missing_definition: Body is the material palate impression driven by alcohol, extract and glycerol; it is not identical to sweetness or viscosity.
missing_descriptors: Rich, broad, powerful, creamy or slightly oily are common texture/body extensions.
editor_conclusion: Keep full body as typical, not universal.

comparison: Low or mild acidity is a stable generic Gewürztraminer trait across official and specialist sources. Falstaff nevertheless notes fine, taut or finesse-rich acidity in several Srem wines, showing terroir, harvest and method can preserve freshness.
independence: Generic reference consensus and actual local tasting evidence provide complementary checks.
missing_definition: Distinguish total/titratable acidity, pH and perceived freshness; «low acidity» is comparative to crisp whites, not necessarily analytically deficient.
editor_conclusion: Keep «usually low to moderate acidity», avoiding an absolute local rule.

comparison: Major wine press directly says dry Gewürztraminer can seem sweeter because low acidity and ripe fruit/aroma shape perception. The book's causal link is directionally right but incomplete: alcohol, aromatic intensity, body and any residual sugar also matter.
independence: General sensory science explanation and multiple cultivar guides converge.
missing_definition: Analytical sweetness is residual sugar; perceived sweetness is the combined sensory impression modulated by acid, alcohol, aroma and texture.
editor_conclusion: Write «low acidity and intense ripe aromatics can make even a dry wine seem sweeter than its residual sugar».

comparison: Falstaff independently documents several 91–93 point Fruška Gora/Srem Traminac wines across multiple styles, so the region is demonstrably strong. No controlled Serbia-wide tasting or comparable current regional series establishes that its wines are the country's best as a class.
independence: The supporting examples are real but mostly come from one critic and one regional tasting cycle; selection bias prevents a national superlative.
missing_definition: «Best» needs a named competition/critic, vintages, style categories and equal sampling from all Serbian regions.
editor_conclusion: Replace with «Fruška Gora is one of Serbia's strongest and most diverse Traminac centres» unless a national comparative ranking is cited.

comparison: Current EN/SR encyclopedias and CANU confirm Serbian cultivation, and Serbian law permits Vranac in several eastern areas; older wein.plus data show only 3 ha nationally. The checked corpus supports south/central/eastern Serbia but not special present-day prominence in Negotinska Krajina.
independence: Academy history, Serbian regulation and an older specialist area table answer different parts of the question and converge only on Serbian presence.
missing_definition: Separate legal permission, actual planted area, historical presence and commercial regional importance; «Negotin, south» collapses these categories.
editor_conclusion: Write «grown in southern and parts of eastern/central Serbia»; attach Negotin only to a documented vineyard or producer, not as an unqualified centre.

comparison: Russian Wikipedia states the exact cognacy and horse meaning; Vasmer links Russian вороной with Serbo-Croatian vran, and the Croatian dictionary defines vranac as a black-coated horse. Wine sources often render it more dramatically as «black stallion».
independence: Two language dictionaries independently secure the etymology; wine encyclopedias and marketing repeat the name gloss.
missing_definition: Literal vranac is a black/raven-coloured horse; «stallion» is a conventional English wine gloss, while the shared root denotes black/raven colour.
editor_conclusion: Keep the Russian cognacy and black-horse explanation; avoid implying that «stallion» is the only literal translation.

comparison: CANU and current EN/SR give blackberry; independent specialist profiles add plum and cherry/dark cherry. The exact trio is representative but not universal and varies among actual wines.
independence: Academy synthesis and independent specialist tasting agree on dark fruit while differing in exact fruit names.
missing_definition: Descriptors are recurrent sensory analogies, not compounds present as literal fruit and not a guaranteed checklist.
missing_descriptors: Blueberry, blackcurrant/cassis, red berries, forest fruit, herbs and dried spice recur widely.
editor_conclusion: Keep as «often blackberry, plum and dark cherry», adding blueberry/blackcurrant as equally established alternatives.

comparison: Chocolate, cinnamon and liquorice recur in mature-wine descriptions; BKWine also finds vanilla/toffee specifically in oak-aged examples. Exact sets differ, and vanilla or wood cannot be attributed to bottle age alone.
independence: The Croatian/promotional maturation formula is textually dependent; independent specialist evidence supports the broader aged/oak profile but not every item in every wine.
missing_definition: Separate secondary/tertiary maturation notes from oak-derived aromas; identify vessel, age, toast and bottle history where possible.
missing_descriptors: Herbs, dried fruit, leather, earth, coffee/cocoa, tobacco, flowers and wood are additional conditional mature-style notes.
editor_conclusion: Keep as possible aged/oaked descriptors, explicitly attaching vanilla to oak influence and avoiding inevitability.

comparison: Decanter, the Croatian profile, regional references and phenolic research support firm or high tannin structure. Independent profiles warn that some examples have rounded or soft tannins despite dark colour.
independence: General references and process experiments converge; maceration and additions demonstrate why structure varies.
missing_definition: Tannin level/concentration, astringency and textural quality are related but distinct; «strong structure» should not imply harshness.
editor_conclusion: Keep «typically firm/marked tannins», not an absolute description of every bottle.

comparison: Decanter and regional sources describe high or crisp acidity, while CANU gives about 5–6 g/L total acidity in wine. Actual perception ranges from lively to balanced depending on wine and style.
independence: Academy analytical baseline and multiple sensory profiles converge on meaningful freshness without fixing one universal value.
missing_definition: Distinguish total/titratable acidity, pH and perceived freshness; «medium-high» is sensory shorthand.
editor_conclusion: Keep «typically medium to high/lively acidity» with vintage and winemaking variation.

comparison: Vranac clearly has strong ageing potential and often responds well to oak or bottle maturation, but current references also recognize multiple styles, including young fruit-led wines; oak and years are options, not necessities for all Vranac.
independence: CANU's multi-style statement, independent specialist profiles and actual young wines contradict the universal necessity while agreeing on maturation benefit for structured examples.
missing_definition: Oak ageing adds flavour and oxygen exposure; bottle ageing evolves structure without wood. They are different processes and should not be bundled as compulsory.
editor_conclusion: Replace «needed» with «structured examples often benefit from oak and/or bottle ageing, which can soften tannins».

comparison: Bright purple and fruit-jam wording appears in Croatian Wikipedia, Vranec World Day and older encyclopedia copies, but these sources are textually related. Current EN/SR/CANU prefer intense ruby or deep colour and berry/spice profiles, and independent writers often find young wines very dark rather than «light».
independence: The apparent agreement is weakened by reuse of one traditional description; independent current profiles support youthfully fruity and purple-toned, not the exact universal formula.
missing_definition: Russian «светло-пурпурный» can be misread as pale; the source tradition means a bright/vivid purple hue, not necessarily low colour intensity.
missing_descriptors: Red berries, strawberry jam, forest fruit, blackberry/blueberry and a blue-violet rim are alternative youthful descriptions.
editor_conclusion: Write «young examples may show a bright purple hue and jammy berry fruit»; do not call Vranac generally pale.

comparison: Ruby evolution, softer structure and increasing aromatic complexity with maturation are credible and widely supported. Only the copied encyclopedia/promotional formula fixes the transition at one or two years, while producer and research evidence shows strong vintage and élevage dependence.
independence: Independent evidence supports direction of change but not the exact timetable.
missing_definition: Age should be counted from harvest or bottling and tied to vessel, oxygen exposure, vintage and wine style.
editor_conclusion: Keep the direction of evolution; replace «after one or two years» with «with maturation» unless a named bottle is meant.

comparison: Several Vranac producer cards specify 18°C and authoritative general guidance gives 16–18°C for structured/ageworthy reds. Exact serving temperature is a target range affected by room, glass and warming after pour.
independence: Named-product recommendations and general professional service guidance converge.
missing_definition: 18°C is the upper end of a service range, not «room temperature» in a warm room.
editor_conclusion: Prefer «serve at 16–18°C» or retain 18°C as a simple target for the named structured style.

comparison: A current Vranac card recommends decanting and general professional guidance supports aeration for young structured reds when the second nose improves. Not every young wine needs a carafe, and duration is bottle-specific.
independence: Vranac-specific producer advice and an official regional service method agree on conditional benefit, not universality.
missing_definition: Decanting may aerate a young wine; in old wine it is often mainly sediment separation and can be harmful if excessive.
editor_conclusion: Write «a young, closed or very tannic Vranac may benefit from short decanting; test in the glass first».
